name: Amira Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Amira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small not-for-profit that fixes up old houses so they're warm and cheap to heat. Retrofit, it's called: we strip out old windows, fit insulation in the walls and lofts, build new frames, that sort of thing. Today I spent four hours on my knees in a loft in Hilltop Road, laying boards and swearing at a joist that wasn't where the drawing said. I'm the junior carpenter on a crew of five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a care worker for eighteen years, home visits, fifteen minutes per person, which is not enough for anybody. My back gave up on the lifting before my heart did. At forty I got a place on a women-in-trades course, and now here I am, three years in. I'm still slower than I want to be, and I still have to look things up that the others just know.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my phone, all day. I take a photo of a joint and ask the AI app if it's right, or I get it to work out the cut list for a frame. My crew lead, Bernie, laughed at first, now he asks me to check his maths. My partner Kofi says I talk to my phone more than to him, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, it's a handy tool and not the end of the world. I'd probably post that, I'm in a few trades groups for women online. Someone always panics, and I'd be the one saying calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I'd hoped it would take some of the heavy lifting off people like me, the ones whose bodies wear out. If it stays as a phone helper, my knees still have to do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep using the app for cut lists and regs, keep at my level two, and keep putting in for the bigger retrofit jobs. We've got about two months of savings, and I'd try to push that to three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. What did you hope AI would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the lofts. Something that carried the insulation rolls up the ladder. Every woman on my course has a bad shoulder or a bad back. That's the job I want a robot to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this picture change anything for the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Ama is fourteen and wants to be a vet, Jojo is eight and wants to be a footballer. In this picture they carry on dreaming like normal, which is fine by me.

S0.say: I'd say it's a handy tool and not the end of the world. I'd post it in my online groups for women in trades, where I'm usually the one telling people to calm down.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I hoped it would take heavy lifting off people whose bodies wear out. If it stays a phone helper, my knees still do the work.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI app daily for cut lists and building rules and keeps working on her level two. Puts in for bigger retrofit jobs and tries to grow savings from two to three months.
S0.quote: If it stays as a phone helper, my knees still have to do the work.
S0.fieldNote: Amira already uses AI every day and sees it as a help, not a threat. Her disappointment flips the usual view: she wanted machines to take the physical strain. Her history in care work, where her body gave out, shapes what she hopes technology will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to make the work better, if workers get a say. Robots doing the lofts, people doing the skilled bits, everybody paid properly. I'd say it in the groups and to Bernie, who'd roll his eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do fine in this one. Retrofit is fiddly, every old house is different, and there's years of work in it. And I'm the one on the crew who already gets on with the tech, which for once makes me useful instead of slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for any course on the new kit, like the thermal cameras and the 3D scanners that measure a room. I'd learn the software side so I could be the person who sets things up for the crew. I'd also join the union branch for retrofit workers, which I've been meaning to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. This one feels like something I can surf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said for once you'd be useful instead of slow. Can you tell me more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For three years I've been the beginner. The lads cut faster, they know the timbers by touch. If the job changes to running scanners and checking robots, suddenly I'm not behind anymore. We'd all be beginners, and I'm a good beginner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernie, a bit. He's fifty-five and hates screens. He's the best carpenter I know. I'd want to help him, not watch him get pushed out because he can't work a tablet.

S1.say: This is the chance to make the work better if workers get a say: robots on the lofts, people on the skilled bits, everyone paid properly. I'd say it in my groups and to my crew lead.
S1.think: I'd do fine in this one, because every old house is different and there's years of retrofit work. For once, being the one who gets on with tech makes me useful instead of slow.
S1.do: Signs up for courses on thermal cameras, 3D room scanners and the software that runs them, aiming to set up kit for the crew. Joins the union branch for retrofit workers.
S1.feel: Calm and even a bit excited, like a wave she can ride.
S1.quote: We'd all be beginners, and I'm a good beginner.
S1.fieldNote: A slow shift in tools turns Amira's weakness, being new, into a strength. Her progressive views show in her focus on who controls the change and in her concern for her older crew lead. Her optimism here seems grounded in the steady flow of retrofit work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for people, fast. Basic income or wages paid during the switch, because two years is nothing. And I'd say the robots should belong partly to the public if public money built the research.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years scares me more than I'd admit online. I'm good with the tech, but if the robot can do the lofts and the joinery and the checking, what's my job? Running one robot instead of five people? That's still four people out, and one of them might be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop paying into the extra pension and keep that money as cash, so we'd have nearer four months. I'd ask the not-for-profit if they'd train me to run whatever kit they buy, so I'm the one kept on. I'd go to every union meeting and push for the law to change. And I'd keep using AI to look for whatever new jobs pop up, because there will be some, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Clear pressure, but I'd feel like I had some moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the two-year timing change things for you compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have to bet on what I already know. No time for a new course. So I'd go all in on being the person who handles the robots on our crew. With more time, I'd have choices. With two years, I've got one shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama, who wants to be a vet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to keep going for now, because animals still need someone gentle. But I'd also be quietly checking if vets are on the list of jobs that go. I'd hate to be the mother who tells her daughter to give up a dream.

S2.say: We need a plan for people fast, with basic income or wages paid during the switch, because two years is nothing. Robots built with public research money should partly belong to the public.
S2.think: Two years scares me more than I'd admit online. If one robot runs the lofts, joinery and checking, that's still four people out of five, and one might be me.
S2.do: Pauses extra pension payments to build cash towards four months of savings and asks her employer to train her to run any new kit. Goes to every union meeting and uses AI to search for new jobs as they appear.
S2.feel: Anxious under clear pressure, but feeling she still has some moves.
S2.quote: Running one robot instead of five people? That's still four people out, and one of them might be me.
S2.fieldNote: Even someone this comfortable with technology sees that being the robot operator only saves one job in five. Her public line is about public ownership and income support, while privately she's planning to be the one kept on. The tension between those two is something she names herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, so don't waste it. Retraining money now, public say in where robots go, and a safety net that's ready before it lands. I'd write to the council about using retrofit as a training ground for the new kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is about right for me. Long enough to learn something properly, short enough to stay focused. I think I could end up as the person who plans the jobs and checks the robot's work, not the one holding the drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a proper course in building surveying, part-time, evenings. I'd keep working retrofit during the day and keep using AI for everything. We'd cut back on the car and drive the old one another few years to keep the savings growing. By year three I'd want to be doing surveys, not lofts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a lot of hope in there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Surveying is quite a step. What makes you think you'd manage it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two things. I already use the scanning apps on my own phone, and I spent eighteen years walking into strangers' homes and working out what's wrong quickly. That's half of surveying. The other half is numbers, and that's what the AI is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, first, around one thousand two hundred for the year. I'd ask the not-for-profit to chip in. If the government offered something, great, but I wouldn't wait for it.

S3.say: Five years is a gift, so don't waste it: retraining money now, a public say in where robots go, and a safety net ready before it lands. I'd write to the council about using retrofit as a training ground.
S3.think: Five years is about right for me, long enough to learn properly and short enough to stay focused. I could end up planning jobs and checking the robot's work instead of holding the drill.
S3.do: Starts a part-time evening course in building surveying in the first year, paying about 1,200 herself and asking her employer to help. Keeps the old car a few more years to grow savings and aims to be surveying by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with a lot of hope mixed in.
S3.quote: I spent eighteen years walking into strangers' homes and working out what's wrong quickly. That's half of surveying.
S3.fieldNote: Amira connects her care work past to a future in surveying in a way that feels earned, not wishful. She'd fund herself first rather than wait for government help, despite her progressive views on public support. Five years reads to her as a workable runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly. Train everybody, share what the robots earn, shorten the working week. I'd join a campaign for that, the kind that knocks on doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years and I'm fifty-three, which isn't old. I'd have time to become a surveyor, work a few years, and see what comes next. The bit I worry about isn't me, it's Ama and Jojo, starting out right when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the surveying course in a year or two, not straight away, and keep doing retrofit while it's busy. I'd help Ama think about her studies, maybe pick something with a bit of everything. I'd join a campaign group for a shorter working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about the kids. For myself, it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year or two with the course, if you know it's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in ten years the jobs might look totally different by year five. I'd rather keep my eyes open and choose when it's clearer. The retrofit work will be there for a while, people's houses are still cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in your plans for Ama's studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want her to study something that gives her more than one door. If vets get robot help, fine, she can still be the person the scared dog trusts. But I'd want her to have a backup, maybe the science side.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this fairly: train everybody, share what the robots earn and shorten the working week. I'd join a campaign that knocks on doors for it.
S4.think: I'd be 53, which isn't old, with time to become a surveyor and see what comes next. I worry less about me than about my kids starting out just as it lands.
S4.do: Starts a surveying course in a year or two while keeping up retrofit work. Helps her daughter plan studies with a backup and joins a campaign group for a shorter working week.
S4.feel: Uneasy, mainly for her children, but fine about herself.
S4.quote: The bit I worry about isn't me, it's Ama and Jojo, starting out right when it lands.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Amira's worry moves from herself to her children, which fits her life stage. She'd hold back from rushing into a course because the picture would keep changing. Her political response grows more ambitious, from income support to a shorter working week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm good with tech, but two years only lets you play the one card you've got. What would help is income while people switch over, and free courses you can do at night, because most of us can't stop working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about bodies. Everybody talks about brains and AI. But in care work, it was my body that ran out first, not my brain. If robots take the heavy work and people still get paid, that's not a nightmare, that's what I was hoping for.

headlineQuote: In care work, it was my body that ran out first, not my brain.
portrait: Amira Mensah is 43 and three years into carpentry on a not-for-profit retrofit crew, after eighteen years as a home care worker whose back gave out. She uses AI on her phone all day for cut lists and checks, and for once that makes her useful instead of slow. She stays calm through the plateau and the slow change, becomes anxious when AGI is two years off, and with five or ten years plans to move into building surveying. Her worry with more warning time shifts to her two children, and her politics lean towards sharing what robots earn.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years only lets her play the one card she already has.
whatWouldHelp: Income while people switch over, and free evening courses for people who can't stop working.
